title: Acute flaccid paralysis and Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute paralysis (onset over hours to days) in India: separating spinal cord from nerve, muscle and junction causes, recognising respiratory danger, and treating Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). Built on the ICMR Approach to Acute Paralysis workflow (October 2019) with the European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society (EAN/PNS) 2023 GBS guideline for diagnosis, respiratory thresholds and immunotherapy, and the enoxaparin label for clot prevention.
findings: Upper motor neuron (UMN) versus lower motor neuron (LMN) triage, causes by pattern, intubation triggers, referral destinations, admission and discharge criteria checked against the ICMR Acute Paralysis STW (October 2019).

GBS diagnostic features, modified Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (mEGRIS), forced vital capacity (FVC) thresholds, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and plasma exchange regimens and timing, and recommendations against steroids and a second IVIg course taken from EAN/PNS 2023.
Enoxaparin prophylaxis dose from the US label.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: Potassium replacement for hypokalaemic periodic paralysis was not dosed in an opened source; follow the local protocol and check serum potassium first (ICMR STW).
Gabapentin and carbamazepine for GBS pain are recommended by EAN/PNS (4.5.2) but no dose source was opened.
Steroid treatment for transverse myelitis is decided after magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at the referral centre; not dosed here.
Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in GBS is not addressed in the opened part of EAN/PNS; the enoxaparin row uses the label dose for immobile medical patients.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute paralysis is weakness of two or four limbs developing over hours to days. The ICMR workflow first separates upper motor neuron signs (spinal cord disease: trauma, tuberculosis, tumour, transverse myelitis, epidural abscess, cord infarct) from lower motor neuron signs (GBS, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, myasthenia gravis, snakebite, myopathy). GBS is an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, often after diarrhoea or a respiratory infection, causing ascending symmetric weakness with absent reflexes that peaks within 4 weeks. The main early danger is respiratory and bulbar failure, so serial bedside breathing tests decide intubation (ICMR STW; EAN/PNS).
keyMechanisms: In GBS, antibodies raised against an infection cross-react with nerve myelin or axons (molecular mimicry).
Demyelination or axonal damage blocks conduction, causing flaccid weakness and lost reflexes.
Phrenic, intercostal and bulbar nerve involvement causes respiratory failure and aspiration.
Autonomic nerve involvement causes swings in blood pressure and heart rate.

symptoms: Weakness of legs or all four limbs over hours to days (ICMR STW)
Tingling and limb or back pain (EAN/PNS supportive features)
Difficulty swallowing, choking on water, breathlessness (ICMR STW admission criteria)
Recent diarrhoea, respiratory infection or fever within 6 weeks (EAN/PNS)
physicalSigns: LMN pattern: reduced or absent reflexes, wasting, sensory impairment (ICMR STW)
UMN pattern: brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, increased tone, sensory level, bladder or bowel incontinence (ICMR STW)
Fatigable weakness or eye-movement weakness: myasthenia or snakebite (ICMR STW)
Bilateral facial weakness (EAN/PNS supportive feature)
redFlags: Unable to complete sentences, low or falling single breath count, short breath-holding time, poor chest expansion: intubate (ICMR STW)
Respiratory rate above 20/min or SaO2 below 95% (ICMR STW admission)
FVC below 20 mL/kg: consider elective ventilation; below 10 mL/kg: intubation almost inevitable (EAN/PNS)
Persistent heart rate above 100/min; bowel or bladder involvement; fever (ICMR STW)
Inability to cough, inability to lift arms above horizontal, neck flexion weakness (EAN/PNS respiratory risk)
precipitants: Diarrhoeal or respiratory infection within 6 weeks (EAN/PNS)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Sensory level, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, early bladder involvement; needs urgent MRI (ICMR STW).
Recurrent episodes, no sensory loss, low serum potassium (ICMR STW).
Fatigable weakness with ptosis or eye-movement weakness; normal sensation (ICMR STW).
Bite history, ptosis and bulbar weakness (ICMR STW).
Proximal weakness, no sensory loss, raised creatine kinase (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Progressive weakness of arms and legs; absent or reduced reflexes in weak limbs; progression for no more than 4 weeks.
Persistent asymmetric weakness, fever at onset, sensory level, extensor plantars, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) above 50 cells/µL.

mEGRIS 0–17 low (under 20%), 18–24 moderate, 25–32 high (over 70%). FVC under 60% predicted, aspiration risk or autonomic instability: intensive care unit (ICU) assessment. Single breath count under 20: consider ICU.
Progressive weakness, unable to walk, unable to swallow, respiratory distress, heart rate above 100/min, fever, or bowel or bladder involvement.
Cause established; weakness no longer progressing; breathing unaided; carers trained in tracheostomy, tube feeding, catheter care, turning and home physiotherapy as needed.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Do early; a normal first-week study does not exclude GBS, repeat if needed (EAN/PNS 4.2.8); ICMR STW refers for these tests.

clinicalManagement.title: Triage at first contact
actions: Pulse, blood pressure and respiration (ICMR STW).
Separate UMN from LMN signs; check serum potassium in LMN pattern (ICMR STW).
Intubate if unable to complete sentences, single breath count low, breath-holding time low or chest expansion poor (ICMR STW).
UMN signs: catheterise for retention and refer to a centre with MRI (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Referral
actions: Suspected GBS with absent reflexes: refer to a district hospital or medical college with plasma exchange or IVIg and a ventilator (ICMR STW).
Myasthenia or snakebite: same intubation criteria; refer for nerve conduction studies, plasma exchange or IVIg and ventilation (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Respiratory and autonomic monitoring
actions: Score mEGRIS on admission; serial FVC if available (EAN/PNS).
ICU assessment for FVC under 60% predicted, aspiration risk or autonomic instability; immediate ICU transfer if FVC falls over 30% in 24 hours (EAN/PNS).

clinicalManagement.title: Immunotherapy for GBS
actions: Unable to walk unaided: IVIg within 2 weeks of onset, or plasma exchange within 4 weeks (EAN/PNS 4.3.5, 4.3.8).
Do not give plasma exchange followed straight by IVIg, a routine second IVIg course, or corticosteroids (EAN/PNS 4.3.8, 4.3.10, 4.3.13).

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care and rehabilitation
actions: Clot prevention while immobile; turning; catheter and feeding care (ICMR STW discharge teaching).
Physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy from the acute phase; continue beyond 6 months if needed (EAN/PNS 4.4.2).
Pain: gabapentinoid or tricyclic, with caution in autonomic failure (EAN/PNS 4.5).

pathophysiology.summary: Jaundice is yellow discolouration from raised serum bilirubin; the ICMR workflow uses a threshold above 1.5 mg/dL. Bilirubin rises when too much is made (haemolysis), when the liver cannot conjugate or excrete it (hepatitis from viruses, alcohol, drugs such as anti-tubercular therapy, or autoimmunity), or when bile flow is blocked (stones, strictures, cancers of the gallbladder, pancreas or bile ducts). In India, systemic infections such as malaria, enteric fever, dengue, scrub typhus and leptospirosis are common causes with fever. Liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and an ultrasound sort most patients; a rising INR is an early sign of liver failure.
keyMechanisms: Haemolysis overloads conjugation: unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises with normal liver enzymes.
Hepatocyte injury impairs uptake, conjugation and excretion: transaminases rise sharply.
Bile duct obstruction backs up conjugated bilirubin: alkaline phosphatase rises, stools pale, urine darkens, itching.
Loss of synthetic function raises INR and signals liver failure.

symptoms: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, viral prodrome (ICMR STW)
Abdominal pain; itching (ICMR STW)
Clay-coloured stools and high-coloured urine (ICMR STW)
Fever (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Scleral icterus
Palpable gallbladder or mass (malignant obstruction)
Signs of chronic liver disease
Pallor and splenomegaly (haemolysis)
redFlags: Altered sensorium (ICMR STW)
Bleeding (ICMR STW)
Recurrent vomiting with dehydration (ICMR STW)
Systolic BP below 90 mmHg (ICMR STW)
INR above 1.5 or rising: early liver failure (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Hepatotoxic drugs including anti-tubercular therapy (ICMR STW)
Hepatitis A or E outbreaks (contaminated water)

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and classify
actions: Confirm bilirubin above 1.5 mg/dL; do LFT, SGOT, SGPT, alkaline phosphatase and ultrasound (ICMR STW).
Check INR; refer if INR above 1.5 or rising (ICMR STW).
Ask about alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs (including anti-tubercular therapy), fever and travel.

clinicalManagement.title: Obstructive jaundice
actions: IV antibiotics if fever or raised white count (suspected cholangitis) (ICMR STW).
IV fluids if dehydrated (ICMR STW).

Refer to a centre with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP); definitive treatment by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) or surgery (ICMR STW).
Biliary drainage or relief of obstruction is of utmost importance in sepsis (NTG 2025).

clinicalManagement.title: Parenchymal (hepatitis)
actions: Maintain hydration; treat symptoms such as vomiting; normal diet (ICMR STW).
Stop alcohol and all non-prescription drugs (ICMR STW).
Thiamine for alcoholic hepatitis (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Isolated raised bilirubin or systemic infection
actions: Haemolysis: folic acid and haematology referral (ICMR STW).
Congenital hyperbilirubinaemia: reassure and refer to confirm (ICMR STW).
Systemic infection: treat the specific illness (ICMR STW).

title: Severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions: SJS/TEN and DRESS (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children with drug rashes in India, focused on the severe reactions — Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) — with first steps for milder maculopapular rashes and fixed drug eruptions. Built entirely on the ICMR Cutaneous Adverse Drug Reactions workflows, Parts A and B (July 2022).

pathophysiology.summary: Cutaneous adverse drug reactions (cADR) range from common, self-limiting maculopapular rashes to life-threatening SJS/TEN and DRESS. SJS/TEN is a T-cell-mediated reaction in which keratinocytes die and the epidermis detaches, usually 4 days to 2 weeks after a new drug, with painful mucosal erosions. DRESS appears later (2–12 weeks) with fever, widespread rash, facial swelling, eosinophilia, lymph node enlargement and liver, kidney or heart involvement. The most important step in every case is to stop all suspect drugs at once and refer severe reactions early (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Drug-specific cytotoxic T cells trigger widespread keratinocyte death and epidermal detachment (SJS/TEN).
Loss of skin barrier causes fluid and protein loss, hypothermia and sepsis — 'skin failure'.
DRESS combines drug hypersensitivity with herpesvirus reactivation, driving eosinophilia and organ inflammation.
High-risk drugs: aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, nevirapine, abacavir, co-trimoxazole, dapsone (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: SJS/TEN care
actions: Skin: dilute potassium permanganate, saline or chlorhexidine baths; leave detached skin in place under non-adherent vaseline gauze; topical mupirocin or fusidic acid on raw areas (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Infection
actions: Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering staphylococci, streptococci and Pseudomonas; adjust to cultures; avoid the suspect drug class (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: DRESS care
actions: Primary care: stop the drug, antihistamines and emollients, refer; do not add unnecessary new drugs (ICMR STW).
Monitor CBC, liver and kidney function at least weekly (ICMR STW).
Severe liver, kidney or heart involvement: tertiary multidisciplinary intensive care; cyclosporine second line if renal function is normal (ICMR STW).

Do not re-challenge in DRESS unless unavoidable; no provocation in active illness or pregnancy (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Hypoglycaemia is the commonest acute complication of diabetes treatment, caused by insulin or sulfonylureas when food, exercise and medicine are mismatched. The brain depends on glucose, so falling levels first trigger adrenergic warning symptoms (sweating, tremor, hunger) and then neuroglycopenia (confusion, drowsiness, seizures, coma). The ICMR workflow treats glucose below 70 mg/dL; severe hypoglycaemia means the person cannot treat themselves, has seizures or is unconscious. Every episode needs a cause and a medicine review (ADA).
keyMechanisms: Excess insulin or sulfonylurea effect suppresses liver glucose output and drives uptake into muscle.
Falling glucose triggers adrenaline release: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger.
Neuroglycopenia causes confusion, behaviour change, seizures and coma.
Repeated episodes blunt warning symptoms, raising the risk of severe events.

pathophysiology.summary: Bacterial skin infections are mostly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci entering through broken skin. Superficial infections (impetigo, folliculitis) need hygiene and topical treatment; deeper collections (boils, carbuncles, abscesses) need drainage; spreading infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis, erysipelas) needs systemic antibiotics, chosen by severity. Diabetes, immunosuppression, scabies and eczema predispose, and recurrent infection should prompt a search for nasal carriage and diabetes (ICMR STW). Severe pain out of proportion, then numbness, with dark skin suggests necrotising infection needing surgery.
keyMechanisms: Breaks in the skin (trauma, eczema, scabies, tinea) let bacteria in.
Staphylococci form pus-filled follicular infections and abscesses.
Streptococci spread through dermis and lymphatics, causing cellulitis and erysipelas with lymphangitis.
Toxin-producing staphylococci cause blistering and peeling in scalded skin syndrome.

pathophysiology.summary: Most sore throats are viral and settle within a week. Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (GABHS) is the main bacterial cause; it matters because untreated infection can lead to rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease and glomerulonephritis, which remain important in India (ICMR STW). The Centor score (no cough, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior neck nodes, fever) decides who gets antibiotics. Dangerous causes — epiglottitis, deep neck space abscess, diphtheria and infectious mononucleosis — must not be missed.
keyMechanisms: Viruses or bacteria infect the pharyngeal and tonsillar mucosa, causing inflammation and pain.
GABHS produces exudate, tender nodes and fever without cough.
Cross-reacting antibodies after GABHS can cause rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.
Spread into neck spaces causes abscesses that threaten the airway.

symptoms: Sore throat, painful swallowing, fever (ICMR STW)
Runny nose, red eyes, cough or mouth ulcers suggest a virus (ICMR STW)
Hoarse 'hot potato' voice (abscess) (ICMR STW red flag)
physicalSigns: Tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes (ICMR STW)
Sandpaper-like scarlatiniform rash (GABHS) (ICMR STW)
Generalised lymph nodes, enlarged liver or spleen (infectious mononucleosis) (ICMR STW)
Grey adherent membrane beyond the tonsils (diphtheria) (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Drooling, high fever, breathing difficulty in a child: epiglottitis (ICMR STW)
Hot potato voice or one-sided tonsil swelling (ICMR STW)
Membrane beyond the tonsils with toxaemia: diphtheria (ICMR STW)
Generalised lymphadenopathy; heart murmur (ICMR STW)
Sore throat with agranulocytosis (for example on antithyroid drugs) (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Smoking and gastro-oesophageal reflux (non-infective sore throat) (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; low or no fever (ICMR STW).
Generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes; rash if given amoxicillin (ICMR STW).
Adherent grey membrane extending beyond tonsils, toxaemia (ICMR STW).
Drooling, stridor or breathing difficulty in children (ICMR STW).
Hot potato voice, one-sided tonsil swelling (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: One point each: no cough; tonsillar exudate; tender anterior cervical lymph nodes; fever.
0–1: no antibiotic. 2–3: antibiotic only if rapid antigen test or throat culture is positive. 4: antibiotic without waiting for tests.
More than 7 episodes in the last year; 5 or more a year for 2 years; or 3 or more a year for 3 years.

pathophysiology.summary: Tuberculous meningitis is the most severe form of tuberculosis. Mycobacterium tuberculosis seeds the brain surface and forms a thick basal exudate that strangles cranial nerves and blood vessels and blocks CSF flow, causing cranial nerve palsies, infarcts and hydrocephalus. It usually presents subacutely with fever for 5 days or more, headache, vomiting and altered sensorium (ICMR STW). Outcome depends on starting ATT and steroids early, so treatment is often started on clinical and CSF grounds before microbiological proof; a negative nucleic acid test does not exclude TBM (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Rich foci near the meninges rupture into the subarachnoid space.
Thick basal exudate entraps cranial nerves (especially VI, III) and blocks CSF flow (hydrocephalus).
Vasculitis of penetrating arteries causes infarcts and hemiparesis.
Inflammation drives raised intracranial pressure and hyponatraemia (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, SIADH).

pathophysiology.summary: Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide can all injure the liver. ATT-induced hepatitis is diagnosed when transaminases rise to 3 times the upper limit with symptoms (or bilirubin 2 times the upper limit with jaundice), or to 5 times without symptoms (ICMR STW). Hepatotoxic drugs are stopped; if TB is severe and treatment cannot pause, a liver-safe interim regimen of ethambutol, a fluoroquinolone and an aminoglycoside is used. When enzymes settle, drugs are reintroduced one at a time — rifampicin, then isoniazid, then pyrazinamide — to find the culprit. Viral hepatitis must be excluded.
keyMechanisms: Isoniazid metabolites (via acetylation) cause direct hepatocyte injury.
Pyrazinamide causes dose-related hepatotoxicity.
Rifampicin can cause cholestasis and enhances isoniazid toxicity by enzyme induction.
Alcohol, malnutrition, HIV, older age and existing liver disease reduce liver reserve.

Severe hepatitis: do not reintroduce pyrazinamide (ICMR STW)

evidenceAudit.scope: Women with heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) in India: assessment, anaemia and endometrial pathology work-up, control of acute heavy bleeding, medical and surgical treatment, and referral. Built on the ICMR Heavy Menstrual Bleeding workflow (December 2025), with the mefenamic acid dose from its US label.
findings: History, examination, pictorial blood assessment chart, investigations, 12 mm endometrial thickness cut-off, age-40 sampling pathway, cancer risk factors, acute tranexamic acid regimen, transfusion threshold, norethisterone and medroxyprogesterone regimens, levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), surgical options and referral checked against the ICMR HMB STW (December 2025).
Mefenamic acid dose taken from the US label (dysmenorrhoea dosing) because the ICMR STW gives none.
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR STW does not define HMB or use the PALM-COEIN classification.
Combined oral contraceptive, iron and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) doses are not given in the STW and are not dosed here.
Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues are not mentioned in the STW.
Some flowchart branches of the STW are ambiguous; the age-40 and 12 mm pathways are summarised as read.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a common cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in Indian women. Causes include fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, ovulatory dysfunction, thyroid disease, bleeding disorders and intrauterine devices. Assessment aims to exclude pregnancy, measure the anaemia, find structural or endometrial pathology (ultrasound endometrial thickness and sampling by age and risk) and treat medically before surgery, especially in younger women (ICMR STW). Acute heavy bleeding with haemoglobin below 7 g/dL needs transfusion and referral.
keyMechanisms: Structural lesions (fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis) enlarge the bleeding surface and impair contraction.
Anovulation leaves unopposed oestrogen, thickening the endometrium (hyperplasia risk).
Increased local fibrinolysis in the endometrium; tranexamic acid blocks it.
Bleeding disorders and anticoagulants impair haemostasis.

clinicalManagement.title: Acute heavy bleeding
actions: IV tranexamic acid 1 g slowly, then oral tranexamic acid (ICMR STW).
Transfuse if haemoglobin below 7 g/dL; refer to a higher centre (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Exclude pregnancy (with consent), then speculum and pelvic examination (ICMR STW).
Haemoglobin, smear, bleeding and clotting times, TSH, ultrasound (ICMR STW).
Endometrial sampling by thickness, age and risk (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Medical treatment
actions: Tranexamic acid during heavy days; add mefenamic acid if painful (ICMR STW).
Cyclical norethisterone or medroxyprogesterone from day 5 for 3 weeks, 4–6 cycles; or LNG-IUS (ICMR STW).
Combined oral contraceptives where contraception is wanted; haematinics; treat thyroid or bleeding disorders (ICMR STW).
Counselling is an important adjunct (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Surgical options
actions: Hysteroscopy-guided procedures, endometrial ablation (ICMR STW).
Hysterectomy if no relief after 3–6 months of medical treatment (ICMR STW).
Refer atypical hyperplasia or malignancy (ICMR STW).
